title: Rifaximin: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Rifaximin
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Rifaximin is a poorly absorbed antibiotic acting mainly within the intestinal lumen.
Bacterial RNA polymerase is the pharmacologic target.
Hepatic encephalopathy recurrence prevention is an established use in appropriate patients.
Systemic infection generally requires an antibiotic with suitable systemic exposure rather than rifaximin.

title: Lactulose: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Lactulose
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Lactulose is a nonabsorbable disaccharide metabolized by intestinal bacteria.
Colonic acidification favors trapping ammonia as ammonium.
Osmotic laxation contributes to stool passage and reduction of intestinal nitrogen burden.
Diarrhea and electrolyte disturbance can occur with excessive effect.

title: Ondansetron (Zofran): Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Ondansetron
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
5-HT3 receptors are blocked by ondansetron to reduce emetic signaling.
Chemotherapy-associated nausea is one common indication for this antiemetic class.
QT prolongation is an important cardiac adverse effect, especially in susceptible patients.
Constipation and headache are commonly reported adverse effects.

title: Metoclopramide (Plasil): Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Metoclopramide
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Dopamine D2 blockade contributes to the antiemetic action of metoclopramide.
Prokinetic activity enhances upper gastrointestinal motility.
Tardive dyskinesia is a serious risk with prolonged exposure.
Renal function and indication affect dosing; a short video is not a substitute for current prescribing information.

title: Misoprostol: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Misoprostol
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Prostaglandin E1 is the endogenous mediator mimicked by misoprostol.
Mucosal protection increases through effects on mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
Diarrhea and abdominal cramping are common adverse effects.
Uterine contraction explains why pregnancy status and indication are crucial to safe use.

title: Sucralfate (Anti Ulcer Drug): Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Sucralfate
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Sucralfate forms a protective complex that adheres to injured gastrointestinal mucosa.
Local action distinguishes it from agents that primarily suppress acid secretion.
Constipation is a recognized adverse effect.
Drug binding can reduce absorption of other medications taken at the same time.

title: Proton Pump Inhibitors: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Proton pump inhibitors
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
H+/K+-ATPase is the gastric proton pump inhibited by this drug class.
Parietal cells are the gastric acid-secreting cells targeted by proton pump inhibitors.
Acid suppression supports healing of acid-related mucosal injury.
Indication review helps avoid continuing treatment without a clear ongoing reason.

title: Histamine H2 Receptor Antagonists: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses and Adverse Effects

notes.text: Histamine H2 antagonists
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
H2 receptor blockade reduces histamine-stimulated acid secretion in parietal cells.
Famotidine is an example of an H2 receptor antagonist.
Cimetidine has more prominent drug-interaction potential than several other drugs in the class.
Renal clearance is relevant to dose adjustment for many H2 antagonists.

title: Antacids: Types, Therapeutic Uses, Adverse Effects and Interactions

notes.text: Antacids
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Neutralization of existing gastric acid is the main action of antacids.
Magnesium salts can cause diarrhea.
Aluminum salts can cause constipation.
Chelation and changes in gastric pH can alter absorption of other medicines.

title: Mucoactive Drugs: N-Acetylcysteine, Guaifenesin and Carbocysteine

notes.text: Mucoactive medicines
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
N-acetylcysteine can break disulfide bonds within mucus.
Guaifenesin is classified as an expectorant.
Carbocisteine is a mucoregulating agent used in some settings.
Underlying cause of cough and sputum production remains central to assessment.
